BUILDING A CI/CD PIPELINE ON AWS: INTEGRATING DEVSECOPS TO PERFORM SECURITY CHECKS BEFORE PRODUCTION DEPLOYMENT In modern software development, deploying source code to a Production environment quickly is no longer enough. An application may function normally while still containing security vulnerabilities, unsafe third-party dependencies, or AWS configurations that have not been properly secured.
If security checks are only performed after an application has been deployed, identifying and fixing issues can take more time, increase costs, and potentially affect system operations.
An effective solution is to integrate DevSecOps into the CI/CD Pipeline on AWS. This approach incorporates security checks throughout the development and deployment process, helping teams identify potential risks before the application is released to the Production environment.
Architecture Overview The CI/CD architecture integrated with DevSecOps uses multiple AWS services to automate application building, security testing, deployment, and system monitoring.
The main components include:
Git: Manages source code and tracks changes made by developers. AWS CodePipeline: Orchestrates the entire CI/CD workflow. AWS CodeCommit: Stores the repository containing the application’s source code. AWS CodeBuild: Builds the application and performs security checks. AWS CodeDeploy: Deploys the application to the target environment. Amazon S3 & AWS CodeArtifact: Store build artifacts and dependencies required during the build and deployment processes. AWS Lambda: Analyzes security scan results and supports the handling of security findings. AWS Security Hub: Aggregates security findings from multiple sources. AWS Config: Monitors and evaluates the configurations of AWS resources. Amazon ECS: Runs the application in Staging and Production environments. CI/CD Process Integrated with DevSecOps The workflow is divided into several stages to ensure that the application is properly checked before being released to the Production environment.
1. Commit – Push Source Code to Git
When developers complete a source code change, they commit and push the changes to the repository.
Git records changes made to the source code. AWS CodePipeline receives an event from the repository to trigger the pipeline. The build and testing stages are executed automatically. 2. Build & Security Scan – Source Code Inspection
AWS CodeBuild builds the application and integrates security testing tools into the workflow.
Two important security testing methods include:
SCA (Software Composition Analysis): Checks third-party libraries and dependencies used by the application. Identifies dependency versions with known security vulnerabilities or potential risks. SAST (Static Application Security Testing): Analyzes source code without executing the application. Detects code patterns or programming practices that may introduce security weaknesses. In the illustrated architecture, the tools used include Black Duck and SonarQube.
3. Deploy – Deployment to the Staging Environment
After the initial build and security checks are completed, the application is deployed to the Staging environment.
AWS CodeDeploy manages the deployment process. Amazon ECS provides the environment in which the application runs. Staging acts as a testing environment before the application is released to Production. 4. Test – Security Testing During Application Runtime
After deployment to Staging, the system continues performing security checks while the application is running.
DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing): Tests a running application by sending requests and analyzing the responses. Identifies vulnerabilities that may appear during application execution. IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing): Analyzes application behavior during runtime. Helps detect security issues based on information collected while the application is operating. In the illustrated architecture, the tools used include Appknox and Veracode.
5. Manual Approval & Production Deployment
Before the application is officially released, the testing results must be collected and evaluated.
Review identified security issues and warnings. Assess risk levels and determine which issues need to be fixed. Require Manual Approval before proceeding with Production deployment. If the application meets the necessary requirements, AWS CodeDeploy deploys it to Amazon ECS in the Production environment. Adding a manual approval stage helps development and security teams maintain better control over the application release process.
Security Monitoring and Control In addition to source code and application testing, the system needs monitoring mechanisms to track activities and detect unusual changes.
Several AWS services support this process:
AWS CloudTrail: Records API activities and changes made within the AWS account. AWS Config: Monitors resource configurations and identifies changes that do not comply with established requirements. AWS Security Hub: Aggregates security findings from multiple services to support risk assessment. AWS Lambda: Analyzes scan results and helps automate the handling of certain security findings. Amazon CloudWatch Logs & Events: Monitors logs, events, and the execution status of the pipeline. Combining these services gives DevOps and Security teams a more comprehensive view of the system’s security status.
Configuration and Access Management A secure CI/CD Pipeline requires more than source code inspection. It must also control access permissions and protect application configuration information.
Important components include:
AWS IAM Role: Grants AWS services the permissions required to perform their tasks. Applies the Least Privilege principle by granting only the permissions that are actually necessary. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: Stores and manages application configuration parameters. Reduces the need to place configuration information directly in source code. Amazon S3: Stores artifacts required during the build and deployment processes. Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service): Sends Email notifications when pipeline activities or security checks generate events that require attention. Scenarios to Validate To ensure that the pipeline works as expected, several practical scenarios should be tested:
Vulnerable Dependencies: SCA detects an unsafe library and generates a warning before deployment. Source Code Security Issues: SAST identifies potential security problems during the build stage. Runtime Application Vulnerabilities: DAST and IAST help detect issues in the Staging environment. Insecure AWS Configurations: AWS Config records resources that do not meet the required configuration standards. Deployment Failure: CloudWatch Logs helps monitor and identify the causes of deployment errors. Security Risk Detection: Security Hub aggregates findings so that DevOps and Security teams can review and resolve them. These scenarios help evaluate the pipeline’s ability to detect, report, and control security risks throughout its operation.
What I Learned Through this CI/CD architecture integrated with DevSecOps, I gained a better understanding that security should be considered an essential part of the software development process rather than simply a final check before release.
Some important lessons include:
Integrating SCA and SAST into the build stage to detect dependency and source code issues early. Using DAST and IAST to test applications in a running environment. Deploying applications to Staging before releasing them to Production. Adding Manual Approval to control important changes before release. Combining Security Hub, AWS Config, and CloudTrail to improve security monitoring and control. Applying the IAM Least Privilege principle to limit unnecessary access permissions. The most important lesson I learned is that DevSecOps changes the security approach from checking applications only after deployment to performing continuous security checks throughout the software development lifecycle.
As a result, organizations can identify vulnerabilities earlier, reduce potential risks, and improve application reliability before releasing software to the Production environment.

Event Report: “AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 – HCMC Watch Party” General Event Information Event Name: AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 – HCMC Watch Party Date: September 29, 2026 Watch Party Location: AWS Office, Ho Chi Minh City Main Event Venue: JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi Organizer: Amazon Web Services (AWS) Format: Hybrid (Live broadcast from Hanoi combined with in-person networking in HCMC) Purpose of the Event Update the technology community in Ho Chi Minh City on the latest trends in Cloud Computing, Generative AI, and Agentic AI. Deepen technical knowledge of cloud architecture and modern application development through live-streamed sessions from AWS specialists. Explore real-world applications of AI Agents for workflow automation, complex task execution, and enterprise system modernization. Discover the role of the AWS service ecosystem in building highly scalable applications. Foster a space for networking and knowledge exchange among local developers, cloud engineers, and AI enthusiasts. Speakers Dr. Werner Vogels – Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Amazon AWS Solutions Architects & Engineering Specialists (Sharing insights across the Builders x AI and application modernization tracks) Event Highlights Keynote – Cloud Computing and the Agentic AI Era The opening session, broadcast live from Hanoi, focused on how cloud computing and artificial intelligence are driving enterprise innovation and digital transformation:
Technology Shift: The evolution from traditional Generative AI to highly autonomous Agentic AI. Workflow Automation: Leveraging AI Agents to orchestrate and execute complex operational workflows. Infrastructure Modernization: Upgrading enterprise applications with a focus on security, scalability, and rapid innovation in the cloud. Builders x AI – Software Development with Agentic AI The Builders x AI track delved into modern methodologies for building and operating software:
Generative AI: AI systems capable of generating diverse outputs such as text, source code, and technical assets. Agentic AI: Architectures enabling AI systems to plan tasks independently, interact with external tools, and execute multi-step workflows. AI-Assisted Software Development: Integrating AI tools into coding, code analysis, testing, and optimizing the software development lifecycle. Cloud-Native Applications: Designing applications to fully leverage elasticity, auto-scaling, and managed cloud services. AI-Driven Application Modernization This theme highlighted the tight integration between AI capabilities and cloud infrastructure in upgrading enterprise technology systems:
Cloud Migration: Migrating and re-architecting legacy infrastructure into modern cloud environments. AI-Assisted Software Engineering: Accelerating system development and maintenance through intelligent automation. Building Data Foundations: Standardizing data architectures to power large-scale AI applications and improve operational efficiency. AWS Community Networking in Ho Chi Minh City Alongside the live-streamed sessions from Hanoi, the Watch Party at the AWS HCMC office served as an in-person hub for the local tech community:
Exchanging hands-on experience implementing AWS services in real-world projects. Discussing the potential and challenges of Generative AI and Agentic AI. Expanding professional networks within Ho Chi Minh City’s developer ecosystem. Key Takeaways Agentic AI Mindset Beyond Traditional Chatbots: Agentic AI combines Large Language Models (LLMs) with APIs, databases, and external tools to solve multi-step problems autonomously rather than merely generating conversational replies. End-to-End Automation: Unlocks the ability to build smarter, more adaptable automation workflows in production environments. Foundational Role of Cloud Computing for AI Comprehensive Infrastructure: The cloud provides the compute capacity, storage, and managed services required to develop, deploy, and operate modern AI workloads. Integration and Scalability: Enables organizations to dynamically scale resources and seamlessly connect diverse software components based on actual demand. Modern Software Development with AI AI as an Enabler, Not a Replacement for Engineering Fundamentals: While AI tools accelerate coding, analysis, and testing, software quality still fundamentally relies on sound system architecture, software engineering principles, and rigorous quality assurance. Value of Tech Communities Continuous Learning: Community events like AWS Watch Parties help practitioners stay abreast of global tech trends, learn from experienced engineers, and sustain long-term career growth. Workplace Application Researching and Experimenting with Agentic AI: Explore combining LLMs with external tools and APIs to build multi-step task automation workflows for personal and workplace projects. Leveraging AI Tools in Development: Integrate AI coding assistants into daily coding, debugging, and testing routines to boost engineering productivity. Designing Cloud-Native Applications: Prioritize AWS managed services to optimize scalability and reduce infrastructure management overhead. Staying Engaged with the Community: Actively participate in AWS meetups and workshops to stay updated on emerging technologies and exchange technical solutions. Event Experience Participating in the AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 – HCMC Watch Party was a valuable experience that gave me a comprehensive view of the intersection between cloud computing and next-generation artificial intelligence. Key highlights include:
Learning from Industry Leaders Listening to technology vision and direction directly from Dr. Werner Vogels (CTO of Amazon) and AWS specialists on the future of Cloud and AI. Gaining a clearer understanding of how major organizations adopt modern architectures to solve operational challenges and accelerate innovation. Technical Insights Across Tracks Sessions in the Builders x AI track offered practical perspectives on the transition from Generative AI to Agentic AI. Understanding how AI Agents coordinate external tools to execute multi-step workflows, along with the underlying data foundation requirements. Applying Modern AI Tools Recognizing the role of AI-assisted development tools in streamlining the Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC), while reinforcing the balance between AI-driven speed and disciplined system design. Networking and Exchange in HCMC The welcoming atmosphere at the AWS HCMC office fostered open conversations and technical exchanges with fellow engineers and peers in the field. Lessons Learned Agentic AI is reshaping how automated software systems are architected and operated. Cloud Computing serves as an indispensable launchpad for building and scaling AI solutions. Maintaining a habit of continuous learning, strengthening core technical foundations, and engaging with professional communities are essential to adapting to the rapid pace of the tech industry. title: Create a gateway endpoint
content:
Open the Amazon VPC console In the navigation pane, choose Endpoints, then click Create Endpoint: You will see 6 existing VPC endpoints that support AWS Systems Manager (SSM). These endpoints were deployed automatically by the CloudFormation Templates for this workshop.
In the Create endpoint console: Specify name of the endpoint: s3-gwe In service category, choose AWS services In Services, type s3 in the search box and choose the service with type gateway For VPC, select VPC Cloud from the drop-down. For Configure route tables, select the route table that is already associated with two subnets (note: this is not the main route table for the VPC, but a second route table created by CloudFormation). For Policy, leave the default option, Full Access, to allow full access to the service. You will deploy a VPC endpoint policy in a later lab module to demonstrate restricting access to S3 buckets based on policies. Do not add a tag to the VPC endpoint at this time. Click Create endpoint, then click x after receiving a successful creation message.

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

title: Prepare the environment
content:
To prepare for this part of the workshop you will need to:
Deploying a CloudFormation stack Modifying a VPC route table. These components work together to simulate on-premises DNS forwarding and name resolution.

One Route 53 Private Hosted Zone that hosts Alias records for the PrivateLink S3 endpoint One Route 53 Inbound Resolver endpoint that enables “VPC Cloud” to resolve inbound DNS resolution requests to the Private Hosted Zone One Route 53 Outbound Resolver endpoint that enables “VPC On-prem” to forward DNS requests for S3 to “VPC Cloud” Click the following link to open the AWS CloudFormation console. The required template will be pre-loaded into the menu. Accept all default and click Create stack. It may take a few minutes for stack deployment to complete. You can continue with the next step without waiting for the deployemnt to finish.
Update on-premise private route table This workshop uses a strongSwan VPN running on an EC2 instance to simulate connectivty between an on-premises datacenter and the AWS cloud. Most of the required components are provisioned before your start. To finalize the VPN configuration, you will modify the “VPC On-prem” routing table to direct traffic destined for the cloud to the strongSwan VPN instance.
Open the Amazon EC2 console
Select the instance named infra-vpngw-test. From the Details tab, copy the Instance ID and paste this into your text editor
Navigate to the VPC menu by using the Search box at the top of the browser window.
Click on Route Tables, select the RT Private On-prem route table, select the Routes tab, and click Edit Routes.

title: Blog 2
content:
AMAZON S3 – A STORAGE AND DATA SECURITY SOLUTION ON AWS In the digital transformation era, data plays an essential role in the operation of businesses and modern information technology systems. From websites and mobile applications to Artificial Intelligence systems, almost every modern application requires a storage solution that is secure, flexible, and scalable.
However, as data continues to grow, traditional storage systems may introduce several challenges, including hardware investment costs, storage capacity limitations, scalability issues, and infrastructure maintenance.
To address these challenges, Amazon Web Services (AWS) provides Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). It is an object storage service that allows users to store and retrieve data with flexible scalability.
In this article, we will explore what Amazon S3 is, its Storage Classes, important data management and security features, and how S3 can be used in Data & Machine Learning architectures on AWS.
1. What is Amazon S3? Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) is an object storage service provided by Amazon Web Services.
Amazon S3 allows users to store and retrieve data through the Internet, AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, and supported APIs without directly managing physical storage infrastructure.
Data stored in Amazon S3 can include:
Images and videos. PDF, Word, and Excel documents. Data backup files. Datasets for Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence. Static website files such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. System logs and analytics data. One of the main advantages of Amazon S3 is its ability to scale according to storage requirements. Instead of purchasing additional hard drives or servers when data volume increases, users can rely on AWS-managed storage infrastructure and pay based on actual usage.
In addition, S3 Standard is designed to provide 99.999999999% (11 nines) of data durability. This is a data durability figure, not a guarantee of 100% service availability.
2. Basic Components of Amazon S3 To understand how Amazon S3 works, we need to become familiar with three important concepts: Bucket, Object, and Object Key.
2.1. Bucket
A Bucket is a container used to store Objects in Amazon S3.
It can be understood as a dedicated storage area for the data of an application or system.
For example, an image management application may use a Bucket named:
my-image-storage-demo
Inside this Bucket, users can store profile pictures, product images, documents, and other types of data.
When creating an S3 Bucket, users need to select an appropriate AWS Region based on data location and system requirements.
2.2. Object
An Object is an individual unit of data stored in Amazon S3.
Each Object typically contains the actual file data and related descriptive information (Metadata).
Examples include:
avatar.jpg report.pdf dataset.csv backup.zip Unlike traditional disk-based storage systems, Amazon S3 uses an Object Storage model, where data is accessed through APIs and Object identifiers.
2.3. Object Key
An Object Key is the unique identifier of an Object within a Bucket.
For example:
images/profile/avatar.jpg
In this case, images/profile/avatar.jpg is the Object Key.
Although this naming structure looks similar to a traditional folder path, Amazon S3 primarily uses prefixes within Object Keys to organize data rather than a traditional physical directory structure.
This makes it easier for users to categorize, search, and manage their data.
3. Amazon S3 Storage Classes Not all data needs to be accessed with the same frequency.
For example, product images on a website may be accessed every day, while backup files from several years ago may only be used when the system needs to be restored.
Amazon S3 provides multiple Storage Classes to support different storage requirements.
3.1. Amazon S3 Storage Hierarchy
Amazon S3 Storage Classes can be grouped according to data access frequency and retrieval requirements:
Frequently Accessed: Data that is accessed regularly and requires low latency. Infrequently Accessed: Data that is accessed less frequently but still requires fast retrieval when needed. Archive: Long-term data storage for information that is rarely accessed and can tolerate longer retrieval times. Figure 1 - Amazon S3 storage hierarchy based on data access requirements.
3.2. Overview of the 8 Amazon S3 Storage Classes
Amazon S3 provides multiple Storage Classes that users can select based on their requirements.
Storage Class Characteristics Common Use Cases S3 Standard Designed for frequently accessed data Websites, images, application data S3 Intelligent-Tiering Automatically optimizes storage tiers based on access patterns Data with unpredictable access frequency S3 Standard-IA Infrequently accessed data requiring fast retrieval Backups and long-term storage S3 One Zone-IA Stores data in a single Availability Zone Re-creatable data S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval Rarely accessed data that still requires fast retrieval Images and long-term records S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval Long-term storage with flexible retrieval times Backups and periodic archives S3 Glacier Deep Archive Designed for rarely accessed data stored over many years Historical records and long-term archives S3 Express One Zone High-performance storage in a single Availability Zone Applications requiring very low access latency Figure 2 - Overview of the eight Amazon S3 Storage Classes and their common use cases.
Some important considerations when selecting a Storage Class:
S3 Standard is suitable for frequently accessed data. S3 Intelligent-Tiering is useful when access frequency cannot be accurately predicted. S3 Standard-IA and One Zone-IA are suitable for infrequently accessed data that still requires fast retrieval. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval is suitable for long-term data that still needs immediate access. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive are designed for long-term storage where longer retrieval times are acceptable. S3 Express One Zone is suitable for applications requiring very low data access latency. Choosing the right Storage Class can help optimize costs. However, users should also consider retrieval fees, request charges, minimum storage duration, and data recovery requirements.
In particular, S3 One Zone-IA and S3 Express One Zone store data in a single Availability Zone. Therefore, availability and fault tolerance requirements should be evaluated before using these classes.
4. Important Amazon S3 Features Besides providing storage capabilities, Amazon S3 offers several features that help manage data lifecycles and improve security.
4.1. S3 Versioning
S3 Versioning is a feature that allows multiple versions of an Object to be stored within the same Bucket.
For example, consider a file named:
project-report.pdf
After updating the report, a user uploads a new version using the same Object Key.
When Versioning is enabled, S3 can retain both the previous and new versions.
This feature is particularly useful when:
Data is accidentally overwritten. An Object is deleted by mistake. A previous version needs to be restored. Changes to stored data need to be tracked. However, previous versions may continue generating storage costs. Therefore, Versioning should be combined with Lifecycle Rules to manage data effectively.
4.2. S3 Lifecycle Rules
S3 Lifecycle Rules allow users to automatically manage the lifecycle of Objects based on predefined rules.
For example, a log storage system may use the following policy:
During the first 30 days: Store data in S3 Standard. After 30 days: Transition data to a Storage Class suitable for less frequent access. After the retention period expires: Automatically delete data according to the configured policy. By using Lifecycle Rules, organizations can reduce manual management tasks and optimize storage costs.
4.3. S3 Encryption
Data security is one of the most important considerations when using Cloud Storage.
Amazon S3 supports data encryption to protect information at rest (Encryption at Rest).
Some common encryption methods include:
SSE-S3: Amazon S3 manages the encryption keys. This is the default encryption method for new Objects uploaded to S3. SSE-KMS: Uses AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to manage encryption keys and provide additional control. SSE-C: Users provide encryption keys with requests, while Amazon S3 performs the encryption and decryption operations. The appropriate encryption method depends on security requirements and organizational key management policies.
4.4. S3 Block Public Access
One common security risk when using Cloud Storage is accidentally allowing public access to private data.
Amazon S3 provides Block Public Access to help prevent configurations that could unintentionally expose Buckets or Objects to the public.
This feature helps control:
Public ACLs. Public Bucket Policies. Configurations that could allow public access. For newly created Buckets, Block Public Access settings are enabled by default.
Recommendation: Keep Block Public Access enabled unless there is a specific requirement and the associated security risks have been properly evaluated.
For applications that need to deliver images or data to external users, solutions such as Amazon CloudFront with Origin Access Control or Presigned URLs can be considered.
5. Basic Guide: Creating and Managing an Amazon S3 Bucket After understanding the concepts, we can practice creating a Bucket and uploading data to Amazon S3.
Requirements: An AWS account or an AWS environment with permission to use Amazon S3.
Step 1: Access the AWS Management Console
Sign in to the AWS Management Console. Search for Amazon S3. Select Buckets to view the existing Bucket list. Step 2: Create an S3 Bucket
Select Create bucket and enter the required information:
Bucket name: Enter a unique name following S3 naming rules. AWS Region: Select an appropriate storage region. Object Ownership: Keep the default settings unless specific requirements exist. Block Public Access: Keep enabled to prevent unintended public access. Versioning: Optionally enable it to explore multiple Object versions. After reviewing the configuration, select Create bucket.
Step 3: Upload Data
Open the newly created Bucket. Select Upload. Choose a test file that does not contain personal or sensitive information, such as demo.txt. Select Upload to start the process. After the upload is completed, the Object will appear in the Bucket’s object list.
Step 4: Check Object Information
Select the uploaded Object to review:
Object Key. Object Size. Storage Class. Metadata. Encryption. Version ID if Versioning is enabled. Step 5: Check Access Permissions
If Block Public Access is enabled, having an Object URL does not mean that everyone on the Internet can access the data.
Users need appropriate permissions through IAM Policies, Bucket Policies, or other authorized access mechanisms.
This is an important concept to remember when developing applications that use Amazon S3.
Step 6: Clean Up Test Resources
After completing the practice:
Delete unnecessary test Objects. Check previous versions if Versioning is enabled. Check Delete Markers. Delete the Bucket after it has been completely emptied. Cleaning up resources helps prevent unnecessary storage costs.
Note: Perform these operations only in an authorized AWS environment and carefully review the data before deleting anything.
6. Real-World Application: Amazon S3 in Data & Machine Learning Architecture Besides common storage applications, Amazon S3 also plays an important role in data processing and Machine Learning systems.
For example, a company wants to build an AI system capable of recognizing and classifying images.
In this scenario, Amazon S3 can be used to store input data, training datasets, models, and processing results.
A sample data structure may look like this:
my-ai-dataset/ | |-- raw-data/ | |-- image_001.jpg | |-- image_002.jpg | |-- processed-data/ | |-- image_001_processed.jpg | |-- train/ | |-- training-data.csv | |-- validation/ | |-- validation-data.csv | |-- models/ | |-- model_v1.pth | |-- results/ |-- predictions.csv Figure 3 - Data & Machine Learning architecture on AWS Cloud using Amazon S3 for data storage and management.
In this architecture, different components can work together as follows:
Amazon S3: Stores raw data, processed data, training datasets, and output results. AWS Glue: Supports data discovery, preparation, and processing. Amazon SageMaker: Supports building, training, and deploying Machine Learning models. AWS Lambda: Can trigger processing tasks when new Objects are uploaded to S3. Amazon CloudWatch: Monitors system activities and the status of different components. For example, when a user uploads a new image to S3, an event can trigger AWS Lambda to start a data processing task. The processed data can then be used in a training or prediction workflow with Amazon SageMaker.
After the process is completed, the model and prediction results can be stored back in Amazon S3 for evaluation and future use.
It is important to understand that Amazon S3 does not directly perform AI model training. S3 provides the storage layer, while processing and training tasks are performed by appropriate computing services.
7. Important Considerations When Using Amazon S3 To use Amazon S3 effectively, several factors should be considered:
Data Security:
Avoid making Buckets containing private data publicly accessible. Apply the Least Privilege principle when assigning IAM permissions. Use Encryption to protect stored data. Regularly review Bucket Policies and Block Public Access settings. Cost Optimization:
Select Storage Classes based on actual access frequency. Use Lifecycle Rules to automate storage transitions. Monitor request, retrieval, and data transfer charges. Review older Object versions when Versioning is enabled. Data Management:
Organize Object Keys using a clear naming structure. Enable Versioning when data recovery is important. Configure appropriate data retention and deletion policies. System Design:
Select an appropriate AWS Region. Identify latency and availability requirements. Integrate Amazon S3 with other AWS services when building Data & AI systems. 8. What I Learned Through exploring Amazon S3, I gained a better understanding of the role of Cloud Storage in building and operating modern technology systems.
Some important lessons include:
Understanding how Amazon S3 organizes data through Buckets, Objects, and Object Keys. Distinguishing between Storage Classes and selecting appropriate classes based on access requirements. Understanding how Versioning helps recover data when unexpected problems occur. Using Lifecycle Rules to automate data lifecycle management and optimize storage costs. Understanding the roles of Encryption and Block Public Access in protecting data. Learning how to create Buckets, upload Objects, and inspect data information through the AWS Management Console. Understanding how Amazon S3 integrates into Data & Machine Learning architectures. The most important lesson I learned is that choosing a storage service is not simply about finding a place to store data. We also need to consider how data is accessed, protected, managed, and optimized throughout its lifecycle.
Amazon S3 is a fundamental service for building Cloud Computing knowledge and exploring more advanced AWS architectures.
9. Conclusion Amazon S3 is one of the fundamental storage services provided by Amazon Web Services.
With its Object Storage model, scalability, multiple Storage Classes, and features such as Versioning, Lifecycle Rules, Encryption, and Block Public Access, Amazon S3 can support many different storage requirements, ranging from frequently accessed application data to datasets that need to be retained for several years.
By learning and practicing with Amazon S3, we can better understand how data is organized, stored, managed, and protected in a Cloud Computing environment.
Discussion Question: When designing a system for storing large amounts of data, what factors should we consider when choosing between S3 Standard, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, and the S3 Glacier storage classes?
I look forward to exchanging ideas and learning more from the AWS Study Group community!

title: Proposal
content:
Driver Drowsiness & Distraction Detection A Driver Drowsiness and Distraction Detection System Combining Edge AI and AWS Serverless 1. Problem & Solution Overview Driver Drowsiness & Distraction Detection is a monitoring system designed for early detection of driver drowsiness or distraction during driving by combining Computer Vision with AWS Cloud, aiming to improve road safety awareness and reduce potential accident risks.
Instead of continuously streaming raw video to the cloud for processing, the system adopts a hybrid Edge AI + AWS Serverless architecture:
At the Edge Device: Facial video frames captured from a webcam are processed locally using OpenCV and MediaPipe Face Mesh to extract behavioral features and analyze states over time. Raw video is never transmitted outside the device. On the AWS Cloud Platform: Only metadata of anomalous events is sent to AWS via Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda for validation, deduplication, storage in Amazon DynamoDB, and historical visualization on a Dashboard (Amazon S3 + CloudFront) secured by Amazon Cognito. 2. Objectives & Scope Project Objectives
Build an on-device computer vision pipeline at the edge to extract facial state metrics including EAR (Eye Aspect Ratio), MAR (Mouth Aspect Ratio), Head Pose, and experimental Gaze Direction. Apply time-series analysis (Temporal Analysis) to accurately identify signs of drowsiness or distraction while minimizing false positives. Deploy a lightweight, secure, and cost-optimized AWS Serverless backend infrastructure to ingest, store, and query event history. Ensure continuous system reliability even during internet outages through a Local Event Buffer and automatic Retry mechanism. Project Scope
Edge AI Processing: Capture webcam frames, detect 478 facial landmarks, extract behavioral features, and classify states using a rule-based engine combined with CSV analysis. The Gaze Direction component remains experimental and requires further evaluation before being used as a primary detection criterion. AWS Cloud Infrastructure: Implement a complete Serverless stack comprising API Gateway (HTTP API), AWS Lambda (Event Writer & Event Reader), Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon Cognito, Amazon S3 (private), Amazon CloudFront (OAC), Amazon CloudWatch, AWS IAM, AWS CloudTrail, and AWS Budgets (along with AWS WAF as an optional edge-protection layer). Testing & Evaluation: Evaluate detection accuracy across varying lighting conditions and camera angles, and verify data synchronization resilience during network disconnection and recovery. 3. Problems to Solve Delayed recognition of drowsiness and distraction cues: Behavioral signs such as prolonged eye closure, frequent yawning, head posture shifts, or gaze deviation occur rapidly, making it difficult for drivers to self-monitor without continuous automated tracking. Limitations of centralized cloud video processing: Streaming real-time video to the cloud demands high network bandwidth, increases response latency, drives up infrastructure costs, and introduces privacy risks regarding driver footage. Data loss or duplication under unstable network conditions: Devices operating inside moving vehicles frequently experience intermittent connectivity. Without local buffering and unique event identification, alert records can be lost or duplicated upon retransmission. 4. Preliminary Solution Architecture 10-Stage System Processing Flow Data Acquisition: A webcam captures the driver’s facial frames and feeds them directly into the local Edge processor (no video is uploaded to AWS). Edge AI Processing: OpenCV combined with MediaPipe Face Mesh (478 landmarks) extracts EAR, MAR, Head Pose, and experimental Gaze Direction metrics. State Analysis: Extracted features pass through Temporal Analysis (using CSV analysis and rule-based candidates) to evaluate drowsiness or distraction states over time. Local Event Buffering: Upon detecting an event, the system generates a unique event_id and stores the metadata in the Local Event Buffer. A Retry mechanism automatically resends unsynced events if network connectivity drops. Cloud Ingestion: The device transmits the event metadata payload via HTTPS POST to Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API). Event Validation & Persistence: API Gateway routes the request to the AWS Lambda Event Writer function to validate the payload. Lambda then executes a Conditional PutItem operation in Amazon DynamoDB keyed by event_id to prevent duplicate entries. Authentication & Authorization: The Dashboard uses Amazon Cognito to handle user sign-up, sign-in, and JWT issuance. API Gateway uses a JWT Authorizer to verify access permissions on incoming requests. History Querying: When a user views event history on the Dashboard, the authenticated request passes through API Gateway to the AWS Lambda Event Reader function to query records from DynamoDB. Dashboard Delivery: The frontend application is hosted on a private Amazon S3 bucket and delivered globally via Amazon CloudFront configured with Origin Access Control (OAC). System Monitoring: Amazon CloudWatch collects API access logs, Lambda logs, error rates, execution durations, and DynamoDB metrics for operational observability and anomaly alerting. Summary of AWS Services Used Functional Group AWS Services Role in Architecture API Ingestion & Compute Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API), AWS Lambda Ingests events from the Edge Device, enforces JWT authorization, and executes write/read logic (Event Writer & Event Reader). Data Storage Amazon DynamoDB Stores event metadata centrally and guarantees idempotency via Conditional PutItem on event_id. Frontend & Content Delivery Amazon S3 (private), Amazon CloudFront (OAC) Securely hosts static web assets and delivers the Dashboard UI over HTTPS. Authentication & Security Amazon Cognito, AWS IAM, AWS WAF (Optional) Manages user accounts and JWT tokens, enforces least-privilege service permissions, and protects the API perimeter. Monitoring & Cost Control Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Budgets Collects logs and metrics, audits account API activity, and triggers alerts on spending thresholds. 5. Implementation Plan & Timeline The project execution roadmap aligns with the 11-week internship schedule (September 21, 2026 – November 30, 2026):
Phase 1 – AWS Foundations & Core Edge Pipeline (Weeks 1 – 8 | Sep 21, 2026 – Nov 13, 2026): Gain hands-on proficiency in core AWS services (VPC, EC2, S3, DynamoDB, IAM, CloudWatch) and Serverless design patterns. Build the initial Edge processing pipeline using a webcam, OpenCV, MediaPipe Face Mesh (extracting EAR, MAR, Head Pose, and Gaze), and rule-based Temporal Analysis. Phase 2 – Architecture Design & Proposal Finalization (Week 9 | Nov 16, 2026 – Nov 20, 2026): Finalize the scope of Driver Drowsiness & Distraction Detection around the Edge AI + AWS Serverless model. Complete the 10-step architecture diagram, design authentication/data flows, and estimate operational costs via AWS Pricing Calculator. Phase 3 – AWS Cloud Deployment, Edge Refinement & Testing (Week 10 | Nov 23, 2026 – Nov 27, 2026): Deploy the full AWS Serverless stack: DynamoDB, Cognito, Lambda (Writer/Reader), API Gateway, S3 (private), CloudFront (OAC), CloudWatch, IAM, CloudTrail, and AWS Budgets. Implement the Local Event Buffer & Retry mechanism, fine-tune Temporal Analysis, and evaluate the stability of Gaze Direction. Test detection accuracy across different lighting environments and camera angles, and validate offline-to-online data synchronization. Phase 4 – Documentation & Final Project Demo (Week 11 | Nov 30, 2026): Finalize project documentation on the Hugo worklog site (GitHub Pages), conduct a live end-to-end demo from Edge to Cloud, and clean up AWS resources upon completion. 6. Budget & Cost Estimation The system leverages an AWS Serverless architecture following a Pay-as-you-go pricing model to minimize operational expenses during development and low-traffic testing, paired with AWS Budgets for proactive spend monitoring and alerts.
Component / Service Estimated Scale / Configuration Pricing Model & Cost Optimization Edge Device (Webcam & Host Machine) Local AI inference via OpenCV + MediaPipe Utilizes existing local hardware; eliminates cloud GPU/EC2 video processing costs. Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Ingests event metadata payloads and serves Dashboard queries Uses HTTP API (more cost-effective than REST API), billed per actual request count. AWS Lambda 2 functions (Event Writer & Event Reader) with lightweight memory Billed per invocation and execution duration (ms); covered largely by the AWS Free Tier. Amazon DynamoDB 1 table storing compact event metadata records On-Demand capacity / Free Tier, scaling read/write costs strictly with actual traffic. Amazon Cognito Handles sign-up, sign-in, and JWT issuance for Dashboard users Free for low Monthly Active Users (MAU) under Cognito’s free tier allowance. Amazon S3 & CloudFront Hosts private static Dashboard assets and serves via CDN Minimal static file footprint results in negligible storage and data transfer charges. CloudWatch, CloudTrail, IAM & Budgets Basic log retention, access governance, and budget alerts IAM is free; configured with concise CloudWatch log retention and early AWS Budgets alerts. 7. Risks & Mitigation Strategies Potential Risk Impact Likelihood Mitigation & Recovery Strategy Loss or instability of internet connectivity in vehicles High Medium Decouple real-time AI inference onto the Edge Device so local alerts operate offline. Implement a Local Event Buffer with an automatic Retry loop to sync queued events once connectivity returns. Duplicate event records during Retry transmissions Medium Medium Assign a unique event_id to every detected event at the Edge and enforce a Conditional PutItem check in Amazon DynamoDB within the Lambda Event Writer to reject duplicate writes. Detection inaccuracy under poor lighting or varied camera angles High Medium Combine multiple behavioral signals (EAR, MAR, Head Pose) through Temporal Analysis rather than single-frame thresholds; test across diverse lighting/angle conditions and isolate Gaze Direction as an experimental feature prior to full adoption. Video privacy exposure and unauthorized Cloud access High Low Never transmit raw video to the cloud (metadata only); enforce least-privilege access via IAM, authenticate users with Cognito JWT, and block direct bucket access using CloudFront OAC. Unexpected AWS Cloud cost overruns Medium Low Adopt a pure Serverless pay-per-use architecture, configure automated spending thresholds via AWS Budgets, and regularly audit usage in CloudWatch / Cost Explorer.

title: Blog 3
content:
AMAZON EVENTBRIDGE SCHEDULER – A SMALL BUT POWERFUL SERVICE FOR AWS PROJECTS During application development, many tasks do not need to be executed immediately. Instead, they must run at specific times or repeat at regular intervals. Examples include sending appointment reminders, updating data every 30 minutes, deleting expired records, or checking system status at the end of the day.
If we use an EC2 instance to handle these tasks, we need to maintain the server, configure its environment, and manage the scheduling mechanism ourselves. This can waste resources when a task only takes a few seconds to complete.
To address this problem, Amazon Web Services provides Amazon EventBridge Scheduler – a serverless scheduling service that automatically triggers AWS services at predefined times without requiring a dedicated server.
In this article, we will explore how EventBridge Scheduler works, its scheduling options, key features, and how to use it to automatically invoke AWS Lambda in a practical project.
1. What is Amazon EventBridge Scheduler? Amazon EventBridge Scheduler is an AWS-managed scheduling service that allows users to create and manage tasks that run once at a specific time or repeatedly according to a defined schedule.
Instead of writing a program to continuously check the time and invoke an API, we only need to create a Schedule, define its execution time, and select a target service. EventBridge Scheduler automatically sends a request to that service when the configured schedule is triggered.
Some AWS services that can be invoked through EventBridge Scheduler include:
AWS Lambda: Execute code for data processing or business logic. Amazon ECS / AWS Fargate: Launch containers to perform tasks that require more computing resources. AWS Step Functions: Start workflows consisting of multiple processing steps. Amazon SNS: Send notifications to subscribers. Amazon SQS: Place messages into a queue for later processing. Amazon EventBridge Event Bus: Publish events for other components in the system. With Universal Targets, EventBridge Scheduler can invoke more than 6,000 API operations across more than 270 AWS services. This provides flexible integration with different components in a Cloud architecture.
Figure 1 - Illustration of how Amazon EventBridge Scheduler creates schedules and triggers target services on AWS.
2. Scheduling Types in EventBridge Scheduler One of the most useful features of EventBridge Scheduler is its support for different scheduling types, allowing developers to choose the option that best fits their application requirements.
2.1. One-time Schedule
A One-time Schedule triggers a task only once at a specified date and time.
Examples:
Sending an appointment reminder to a user. Automatically sending a notification 24 hours after a user registers. Triggering a task on an order’s expiration date. This option is suitable for tasks that only need to run once rather than repeatedly.
2.2. Rate-based Schedule
A Rate-based Schedule executes tasks repeatedly at fixed time intervals.
Example:
rate(30 minutes) This expression instructs EventBridge Scheduler to invoke the target every 30 minutes.
Common use cases include:
Periodically updating application data. Checking system status. Aggregating data at regular intervals. Automatically synchronizing information between services. 2.3. Cron-based Schedule
A Cron-based Schedule uses Cron expressions to define execution times based on minutes, hours, days, or days of the week.
Example:
cron(0 8 ? * MON *) This expression represents 8:00 AM every Monday in the time zone configured for the Schedule.
Another useful feature is local time zone support. For example:
Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh This allows developers to configure schedules based on Vietnam local time without manually converting every execution time to UTC.
3. Key Features of EventBridge Scheduler EventBridge Scheduler is more than just a timer. It also provides built-in mechanisms that improve system reliability and reduce operational overhead.
3.1. No Need to Maintain a Server (Serverless)
This is one of the most noticeable advantages of using EventBridge Scheduler.
Imagine an application that needs to execute a task for a few seconds every 30 minutes. If we use EC2, the instance may still need to run continuously even though it spends most of its time doing nothing.
With EventBridge Scheduler, AWS manages the underlying scheduling infrastructure. Developers only need to configure the Schedule and Target without operating a dedicated server.
This helps:
Reduce server administration tasks. Eliminate the need to write programs that continuously check the time. Reduce idle infrastructure resources. Scale more easily as the number of schedules increases. 3.2. Retry Policy – Automatically Retry Failed Invocations
In real-world applications, a target service may temporarily become unavailable, experience request throttling, or fail to process a request.
EventBridge Scheduler supports Retry Policy to automatically retry failed target invocations.
Some important configuration limits include:
The maximum retention time for an unprocessed event can be configured up to 24 hours. The maximum number of retry attempts can be configured up to 185. Retry attempts use exponential backoff to increase the waiting time between attempts. This gives the system additional opportunities to complete a task when the target experiences a temporary failure.
3.3. Dead-letter Queue (DLQ)
If Scheduler still cannot deliver an event to the target after the configured retry attempts, developers can configure an Amazon SQS Queue as a Dead-letter Queue.
Events that cannot be delivered successfully are sent to the DLQ for further investigation and processing.
For example, a notification task may fail because the Lambda Function is temporarily unavailable. Instead of losing track of the event, its information can be stored in the DLQ so the development team can investigate the cause and take appropriate action.
3.4. Flexible Time Window
Imagine thousands of schedules configured to run at 12:00 AM. If all requests are sent to the target system at the same time, the system may experience a sudden increase in workload.
Flexible Time Window allows AWS to distribute invocations across a configured time window.
For example, if a five-minute window is selected, Scheduler can invoke the target within five minutes after the scheduled time.
This feature is suitable for tasks that do not require execution at an exact moment. If a task needs to run closer to its scheduled time, Flexible Time Window can be turned off.
3.5. Time Zone Support and Centralized Management
EventBridge Scheduler allows schedules to be managed through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, and SDKs.
Users can also select a local time zone when creating a schedule, such as Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh.
For projects with multiple automated tasks, Schedule Groups can be used to organize schedules by purpose:
development-schedules production-schedules notification-schedules This organization makes it easier to manage and monitor schedules as a project grows.
4. Practical Example: Automatically Invoking AWS Lambda Every 30 Minutes Imagine that our project has a periodic data collection feature. Every 30 minutes, the system needs to invoke a Lambda Function to retrieve new data and update the database.
There are two possible approaches:
4.1. Traditional Approach: Using EC2 and Crontab
If we use EC2, we need to perform the following tasks:
Launch an EC2 instance and configure its operating system. Install the required environment, such as Python, Node.js, or AWS CLI. Write a script to invoke the Lambda Function. Configure crontab to execute the script every 30 minutes. Manage logs, troubleshoot failures, and maintain the server. Attach an IAM Role to EC2 to grant permission to invoke Lambda. This approach can work, but it requires maintaining a server continuously even when the actual task only takes a few seconds.
4.2. Using EventBridge Scheduler
With EventBridge Scheduler, the workflow becomes much simpler and can be configured directly through the AWS Management Console.
Step 1: Create a Schedule
Open the AWS Management Console, navigate to Amazon EventBridge, and select Scheduler to create a new Schedule.
Choose Recurring schedule, then select Rate-based schedule and enter:
rate(30 minutes) If the task needs to run according to Vietnam local time, select Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh in the Schedule configuration.
Step 2: Select the Target
Choose AWS Lambda as the target service and specify the Lambda Function that needs to be invoked.
Step 3: Configure the Execution Role
Create or select an IAM Execution Role that allows EventBridge Scheduler to invoke the Lambda Function.
AWS can help create the Role during the configuration process. However, developers should review the granted permissions and ensure that the Role only has the permissions it needs.
Step 4: Configure Failure Handling
Depending on project requirements, developers can configure:
Retry Policy to automatically retry failed target invocations. Amazon SQS DLQ to store events that cannot be delivered successfully. Flexible Time Window when the task does not require execution at an exact scheduled time. After completing the configuration, EventBridge Scheduler automatically invokes Lambda according to the defined schedule without requiring a dedicated EC2 instance.
4.3. Monitoring the Execution
To verify whether the system is working correctly, developers can use:
Amazon CloudWatch Metrics: Monitor invocation counts, failed invocations, and other Scheduler-related metrics. AWS Lambda Monitor: Check invocation counts, execution duration, and Lambda errors. CloudWatch Logs: Inspect logs generated by the Lambda Function and any Scheduler logging that has been configured. Amazon SQS DLQ: Inspect events that could not be successfully delivered to the target service. Regular monitoring helps detect failures early and ensures that automated tasks run as expected.
5. Important Considerations 5.1. Pricing and Free Tier
According to the AWS pricing page, EventBridge Scheduler provides up to 14 million free invocations per month. After the free usage allowance, charges are based on the number of invocations and the AWS Region being used.
For student labs, academic projects, and applications with a relatively small number of scheduled tasks, this free usage allowance is useful for experimentation.
However, developers should remember that target services such as Lambda, ECS, SQS, and CloudWatch may have their own charges. Therefore, the entire automation workflow should not be assumed to be completely free.
5.2. EventBridge Scheduler vs. EventBridge Rules
Previously, many developers used EventBridge Rules to create scheduled tasks. However, these two features serve different purposes:
EventBridge Scheduler: Designed for independent scheduling tasks. It supports One-time, Rate, and Cron schedules, along with Retry Policy, DLQ, and Flexible Time Window. EventBridge Rules: Primarily designed to filter events on an Event Bus and route matching events to targets based on Event Patterns. Rules also support Scheduled Rules. AWS recommends EventBridge Scheduler for new scheduling requirements because it provides more specialized scheduling features and scalability.
5.3. Security and Operational Best Practices
Grant IAM Execution Roles only the minimum permissions required. Avoid disabling Retry Policy and DLQ without considering the importance of the scheduled task. Monitor CloudWatch Metrics to detect failed invocations. Delete or configure automatic deletion for completed One-time Schedules if they are no longer needed. Review the costs of both Scheduler and the target services it invokes. 6. Conclusion Amazon EventBridge Scheduler is a small service that solves a very common application development problem: automatically executing tasks according to a schedule without maintaining a dedicated server.
With its integration with multiple AWS services, different scheduling options, Retry Policy, Dead-letter Queue, and Flexible Time Window, Scheduler simplifies the implementation of automation workflows.
For student projects and serverless applications, this is a service worth learning and applying. Instead of building a scheduling system from scratch, developers can use an AWS-managed service to reduce development time and focus more on the application’s core logic.
Thank you for reading! If you have used EventBridge Scheduler in your own projects or have experience optimizing scheduled tasks on AWS, feel free to share your thoughts and practical experiences!

title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.

Secure Hybrid Access to S3 using VPC Endpoints Overview AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity to AWS services from VPCs and your on-premises networks, without exposing your traffic to the Public Internet.
In this lab, you will learn how to create, configure, and test VPC endpoints that enable your workloads to reach AWS services without traversing the Public Internet.
You will create two types of endpoints to access Amazon S3: a Gateway VPC endpoint, and an Interface VPC endpoint. These two types of VPC endpoints offer different benefits depending on if you are accessing Amazon S3 from the cloud or your on-premises location
Gateway - Create a gateway endpoint to send traffic to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB using private IP addresses.You route traffic from your VPC to the gateway endpoint using route tables. Interface - Create an interface endpoint to send traffic to endpoint services that use a Network Load Balancer to distribute traffic. Traffic destined for the endpoint service is resolved using DNS. title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
General Assessment 1. Working Environment
The learning and internship environment at the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) program is very open, dynamic, and encourages students to take initiative in research. Team members are always willing to discuss ideas, share resources, and provide timely technical troubleshooting support during hands-on labs and project implementation. Adding a few more networking or interactive sessions among internship groups would make team bonding even stronger.
2. Support from Mentor / Team Admin
The mentor and team admins provided dedicated guidance and clear direction from the early stages of learning foundational AWS services to finalizing the capstone topic and system architecture. Rather than giving direct answers right away, they consistently asked thought-provoking questions so I could analyze the pros and cons of each option, which helped me understand the underlying technical principles deeply. The team admins were also very supportive with reporting workflows, templates, and answering inquiries promptly throughout the internship.
3. Alignment Between Assigned Tasks and Academic Major
As an Artificial Intelligence major, I found the internship content highly complementary to my university studies. Building the Driver Drowsiness & Distraction Detection project allowed me to combine the Computer Vision knowledge (OpenCV, MediaPipe) I learned at school with AWS Serverless cloud infrastructure to deliver an end-to-end system capable of real-world authentication, storage, and monitoring.
4. Learning Opportunities & Skill Development
Throughout the internship, I not only gained hands-on proficiency in deploying and integrating core AWS services (IAM, API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, Cognito, S3, CloudFront, CloudWatch, etc.) but also developed an architectural mindset focused on security and cost optimization. In addition, maintaining weekly Worklogs, managing report documentation via GitHub/Hugo, and presenting architectural designs significantly improved my personal discipline and technical writing skills.
5. Culture & Team Spirit
The spirit of knowledge sharing and mutual support within the team is very positive. Everyone respects individual perspectives and provides constructive feedback during progress reviews and system testing, creating a comfortable atmosphere that helped me become more confident in collaborative work.
6. Policies / Benefits for Interns
The program offers a flexible roadmap and schedule well-suited for students. Having access to well-structured documentation, practical hands-on labs, and thematic sharing sessions from the FCAJ team served as valuable support for my learning and professional growth.
Additional Questions What are you most satisfied with during your internship?
What satisfies me most is designing and deploying a complete end-to-end data pipeline for the capstone project—from the Edge AI device to AWS Serverless infrastructure—while mastering how to enforce security (JWT, IAM, OAC), prevent data loss or duplication during network outages, and manage operational costs rather than stopping at a local model prototype.
What do you think the program/organization should improve for future interns?
The program could include a dedicated wrap-up session covering common configuration pitfalls (such as IAM permissions, API Gateway CORS settings, or cost guardrails) right before the capstone project phase so future interns can save troubleshooting time and deploy with greater confidence.
If recommending to friends, would you advise them to intern here? Why?
I would definitely recommend the First Cloud AI Journey program to my friends, especially students looking for practical exposure to AWS cloud computing. The program provides a clear roadmap from foundational concepts to real-world project deployment, attentive mentorship, and practical experience in building complete systems.
Suggestions & Expectations Do you have any suggestions to improve the internship experience?
Organizing cross-team mock demo sessions before the final submission week would give interns the opportunity to observe different architectural approaches and refine their technical presentation skills.
Would you like to continue engaging with this program in the future?
I would love to stay connected with the AWS Study Group / FCAJ community to continue learning more advanced topics in Cloud Security and system architecture going forward.
Other feedback (open sharing):
I would like to express my sincere gratitude to the First Cloud AI Journey admin team for their dedicated guidance, support, and for creating the best possible conditions for me to successfully complete this internship.
